words.translation: Thus — pointing back over all eighteen hundred and some syllables that have just been recited.

morphology.note: Indeclinables take no endings. The final m appears here as anusvāra because a sibilant follows: evam + śrī → evaṃ śrī.

words.note: The word that turns the preceding thousand names into a completed object. Everything before this line was the hymn; from here the text speaks about the hymn.

words.translation: …belonging to the goddess Śrī Lalitā, whose name the hymn has just finished pronouncing for the thousandth time.

morphology.note: Carries no ending of its own: it is the prior member of a compound whose case is supplied at the far end, by devyāḥ.

children.gloss: light, splendour, prosperity; as a prefix to a name, an honorific
playful, charming, lovely — from √lal, to play or sport; her proper name

words.note: Printed as a separate word, but grammatically it is bound to devyāḥ: the two together are one compound in the genitive. The same name closed the thousand two words earlier as lalitāmbikā, so it is heard twice in a single line — once as the last of the names, once as the owner of them all.

words.translation: …of the goddess — the genitive that the whole line hangs from.

morphology.note: The genitive singular of devī is devyāḥ. The visarga is not missing: final -āḥ regularly loses it before a voiced sound, and nāmnāṃ begins with n, so devyāḥ nāmnāṃ is written devyā nāmnāṃ.

words.note: Worth pausing on, because the written form devyā is identical to the instrumental singular and is easily misread as "by the goddess" — which would make her the singer rather than the subject. The singers are plural, and named by the verb at the end of the line.

words.translation: …of the names — all of them, taken together.

morphology.note: Weak stem nāmn- plus the genitive plural -ām gives nāmnām, written with anusvāra before the following s: nāmnāṃ sāhasrakam.

words.note: A partitive genitive depending on sāhasrakam: not "the thousand names" as a loose phrase but "the thousand-fold collection of the names". Sanskrit is being precise about the fact that the thousand is a grouping imposed on the names, which is why the count can be a matter of argument at all.

words.translation: …the full thousand of them, as one thing.

morphology.note: A secondary derivative: sahasra, a thousand, with vṛddhi of the first vowel and the suffix -ka, giving a noun for the collection rather than the number.

words.note: The object of the verb, and singular — they did not sing a thousand names, they sang one thousand-fold thing. That grammatical choice is the reason the hymn is treated in practice as a single unbreakable recitation rather than a list one may sample from.

words.translation: …they sang. The hymn's last word puts the whole of it in the past tense and in someone else's mouth.

morphology.rootMeaning: to sing, chant, recite in song
morphology.note: Reduplicated perfect of √gai: the root vowel weakens and the reduplicating syllable ja- is prefixed, giving jagau in the third singular and jaguḥ in the third plural.

words.note: Plural, and no subject is stated, because the subject was established when the hymn began: the eight Vāgdevatās, the goddesses of speech, who were commissioned to compose it. The last act of the text is to disown its own authorship — it does not say "I have praised you" but "thus they sang", so that the reciter joins a performance already under way rather than starting one.
